tagline: A Pee Dee landscape of wintering waterfowl and a hydropower lake
intro: Grassy Island Crossing appears among the Piedmont routes in North Carolina’s scenic-byways guide. The Pee Dee landscape includes bottomland hardwood forest, pine woods and cropland at Pee Dee National Wildlife Refuge.

The river changed when a dam created Blewett Falls Lake for hydropower in the early 20th century, covering the former falls. In 1963, the wildlife refuge was established to provide winter habitat for geese and other migratory waterfowl.

Ansonville lies about a mile west of the Pee Dee River. The refuge occupies land along the river in Anson and Richmond counties. Blewett Falls Lake extends into both counties too, with 34 miles of shoreline and no bridge spanning its water.

moments.title: Ansonville
moments.text: Ansonville’s early college served a narrowly defined group: the daughters of local planters, all white women. The North Carolina Legislature created Carolina Female College here in 1850, six years after the town was settled. The Civil War brought the school’s closure, although the date is disputed between 1862 and 1867. The town lies on Anson County’s northern edge, about a mile west of the Pee Dee River.

moments.title: Pee Dee National Wildlife Refuge
moments.text: Wintering birds depend here on a managed landscape of fields, water and forest. Established in October 1963 for geese and other migratory waterfowl, the refuge lies a few hundred yards from the private Lockhart Gaddy Wild Goose Refuge. In the 1950s, Gaddy’s pond wintered more than 10,000 Canada geese annually. At Pee Dee, cooperative farming, managed water levels and Brown Creek’s bottomland hardwood forest provide habitat. Wintering waterfowl numbers vary greatly, but can exceed 10,000 birds in a year. The refuge also supports nesting neotropical migratory birds, as well as bobwhite quail and wild turkeys.

moments.title: Blewett Falls Lake
moments.text: Blewett Falls Lake occupies the former falls of the Great Pee Dee River. A dam created the reservoir for hydropower in the early 20th century; its name preserves that of the falls and the early local family they honored. The lake spreads across 2,560 acres in Anson and Richmond counties. It is the southernmost and widest lake in the Uwharrie Lakes chain. Along its 34 miles of shoreline, no bridge spans the lake.
